Comparison

Fully Adhered vs. Mechanically Attached Membranes

The attachment decision under every single-ply roof — wind performance, cost, fluttering, and the building conditions that pick the method.

Source verification in progress Updated July 15, 2026 2 min read Editorial standards · Report an error
Source verification in progressSources for this page are still being verified. Details may change.

Key takeaways

  • Attachment method affects wind performance, energy, acoustics, and price — often more than membrane brand does.
  • Mechanically attached is faster and cheaper; fully adhered is calmer, tighter, and generally the high-wind and high-performance choice.
  • Wind uplift design is code-driven engineering: corner and perimeter zones govern, and the answer is calculated, not chosen.
  • Deck type and condition can decide the method before preference gets a vote.

The two methods

  • Mechanically attached (MA): membrane fastened in rows through to the deck; fasteners hidden in seams. Fast, economical, deck-dependent.
  • Fully adhered (FA): membrane glued continuously to the substrate. No point loads, no flutter, higher labor and adhesive cost.

(Ballasted systems — loose-laid under stone — are a third path with weight and wind-zone constraints; induction-welded hybrids blur the categories. Both worth asking about.)

Side by side

CriterionMechanically attachedFully adhered
First costLowerHigher
Wind upliftEngineered rows; flutter betweenUniform load path; premium in high-wind
Membrane movement/noiseFlutter possibleNone
Air/vapor behaviorBillowing can pump airTighter assembly
Deck requirementsNeeds fastener-holding deckNeeds clean, sound, dry substrate
Repairs/reroof laterFastener pattern knownAdhered layers harder to separate

What actually decides it

  1. Wind engineering. Uplift pressures from code (ASCE 7) size everything. In hurricane and high-rise-edge zones, FA (or enhanced MA/induction systems) usually carries the calculation; in ordinary zones, MA passes economically.
  2. Deck. Steel deck holds fasteners well (MA-friendly); concrete favors adhered; gypsum/tectum decks often can’t hold screws at all — the deck decides.
  3. Building use. Sound-sensitive occupancies notice MA flutter drum; FA is silent.
  4. Budget honesty. MA’s savings are real; whether they’re worth it is a wind-zone and risk-posture question, not a universal.

Common mistakes

  1. Comparing an FA bid to an MA bid as if they were the same product at two prices.
  2. Value-engineering corner and perimeter enhancement out of an MA spec — those zones are where roofs leave buildings.
  3. Adhering over a substrate that failed (or never had) adhesion testing.

FAQ

Which is better in a hurricane? Neither “wins” — the assembly either meets calculated uplift or it doesn’t. FA and enhanced-fastening systems more commonly clear high-wind numbers; demand the uplift calculation and tested-assembly listing (FM/UL) either way.

Does fully adhered last longer? Not inherently; it removes flutter fatigue and point stresses, which helps at the margins. Installation quality still dominates.
